Large-Cap Institutional
Ownership 1Q26: Mega-Cap
Tech Under-Ownership Narrows

The gap between Mega-cap tech S&P weighting and institutional ownership narrowed 12bps in 1Q, with mega-cap tech now 125bps under-owned vs. -137bps in 4Q. The rest of large-cap tech is modestly over-owned at +32bps. NVDA remains the most under-owned, followed by AAPL, MSFT, AMZN and GOOGL.
Mega-cap Tech under-ownership vs the S&P 500 modestly narrowed to -125bps from -137bps at 4Q25 end.
Outside of mega-cap Tech stocks, the spread between institutional ownership and S&P 500 weighting was +32bps, in-line with last quarter.
NVDA remains the most under-owned large-cap tech stock vs. S&P 500 at -2.39%, followed by AAPL (-2.32%), MSFT (-1.86%), and AMZN (-1.24%).
■ SNDK is still the most "over-owned" large-cap tech stock at +2.16% vs. S&P 500, more than 2x STX, the next most over-owned stock behind SNDK.
Institutional positioning in large-cap tech favors AI infra bottlenecks, with relatively high memory/storage ownership and low software ownership exiting 1Q26.

Mega-cap Tech stocks are modestly less under-owned vs. the S&P 500 exiting 1Q26 than at 2025 year-end; NVDA remains the most "under-owned" large-cap tech stock, while SNDK is the most "over-owned" (Exhibit1). Leveraging 13Fs filed for the end of 1Q26, most mega-cap technology stocks remain under-owned relative to their weighting in the S&P 500, with NVDA (-2.39%), AAPL (-2.32%), MSFT (-1.86%) and AMZN (-1.24%) the most under-owned of the mega-cap tech stocks we track. Conversely, SNDK (+2.16%), STX (+0.84%) and CRM (+0.63%), are the most over-owned technology stocks we track relative to their weighting in the S&P 500. On average, the spread between active institutional ownership and S&P 500 weighting for the largest technology companies in the US by market cap - NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, META, and TSLA - was -125bps exiting 1Q26 (Exhibit 2) vs. -137bps at the end of 4Q25, showing a modest narrowing of mega-cap under-ownership over the last 90 days. For the remaining 21 large-cap tech stocks we track, the spread between institutional ownership and S&P 500 weighting exiting 1Q26 was +32bps, in-line with 4Q25.

At the stock level, there are three key observations from the 1Q26 13-F data.

First, NVDA remains the most under-owned large-cap tech stock we track as of 1Q26 (Exhibit 2), with the gap between NVDA's S&P 500 weighting and institutional ownership narrowing Q/Q by just 18bps, ending 1Q26 at -2.39%, near all-time highs. Second, exiting 1Q26, institutional active manager ownership remains notably high (vs. the S&P 500) in large cap memory/storage-related names - SNDK, STX, LRCX, KLAC, and WDC - but notably low in software stocks - IBM, ORCL, PANW, NOW and ADBE, illustrating a continued clear institutional bias towards AI 'picks and shovels' / bottlenecks in 1Q. Finally, we'd highlight that SNDK's institutional ownership has been steadily increasing since its re-listing in 1Q25, and even after its inclusion into the S&P 500 in 4Q25, SNDK has the widest gap between institutional ownership and S&P 500 weighting among any other large-cap tech stock we track, with the "over-ownership" gap exiting 1Q26 at +2.16%, more than 2x STX, the next most "over-owned" large cap tech stock we track.

Exhibit 2: Of the large cap stocks we evaluate, NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, AMZN, and GOOGL are currently the most under-owned in actively managed portfolios vs. the S&P 500, while SNDK, STX, CRM, and LRCX are the most over-owned.

Why does this data matter? Each quarter, we track ownership data for 28 of the largest cap tech companies across MS's US technology equity research coverage, which is based on each company's average weighting within the top 100 actively managed institutional portfolios relative to that same company's weighting in the S&P 500. A quant analysis of this historical ownership data indicates that, on average, after adjusting for market cap and earnings beats, there is a statistically significant relationship between low active ownership relative to the S&P 500 and future stock performance. This indicates that on average, stocks appear to experience a technical pull higher when active ownership is much lower than the market, and vice versa.

With the most elongated iPhone replacement cycles, new AI features rolling out around the world, and a renewed focus on device form factor changes, we believe Apple can accelerate iPhone growth starting in FY26, with replacement cycles peaking as aged installed base starts to upgrade. When combined with consistent, double digit services growth and moderate operating leverage, we believe Apple can earn $8.89 in FY26 and $10.23 by FY27. Memory cost dynamic could create uncertainties in the near term. Longer-term, investments in AI, payments, cloud, health, and home, and long runway to grow spend per user from $1/day today are key arguments for sustained long-term growth and value creation.

Execution on newer offerings (like click to message) could also contribute to higher than expected growth. Declines in engagement and/or evidence of Reels monetization ramping more slowly than expected could lead to lower growth and greater uncertainty. We also watch for any macro uncertainty, regulation that limits META's ability to target ads, Reality Labs losses widen more materially than expected, and higher capital intensity from mis-execution around the data center build. Any additional opex and capex could weigh on operating income growth and FCF.

IBM has gained credit for driving more consistent performance in recent years and shifting its portfolio to more recurring Software and Services. The acquisition of HashiCorp combined with a mainframe/ELA cycle is resulting in growth accelerating in 2025, but also creates risk of a deceleration in 2026. This risk, among others, is what supports our $225 price target. Yet, the market is clearly also focused on Quantum, and given the re-rating we have seen from pure-play quantum stocks, IBM's early Quantum leadership has upside optionality. Balancing these facts is what drives our EW-rating, with mis-execution the key bear case risk.
